2026 SEMA Show • 2027 Toyota Crown Signia Gets GT-S Concept Treatment for SEMA, Becomes a Sleek Wagon
Lambo's Revuelto SV Gets the Ad Personam Treatment, Looks Like an Exotic Pumpkin Late for Halloween
10 photos
Photo: Instagram | lamborghinimiami
Actually, it’s not late for Halloween, because images of this supercar were shared online before the holiday. We were just late to catch them. But better late than never, right?
First things first, let’s dedicate a few lines to the actual model, which is the latest and greatest Lambo that money can buy. It is called the Lamborghini Revuelto SV , with its suffix standing for SuperVeloce, and “veloce” is Italian for “speed,” in case you forgot. The company’s fastest and most powerful model ever debuted when it was still summer in the northern hemisphere, as it was unveiled in August during the 2026 Monterey Car Week.
This is the latest in a long line of SV models, which also included the SV versions of the Aventador, Murcielago, Diablo, and Miura. It features a revised suspension with manually-adjustable dampers that were derived from GT3 racing, and this move is said to have increased the agility and lateral grip by 17 and 10 percent, respectively over the regular Revuelto. It features center locking wheels, 20 inches at the front and 21 inches at the rear, backed up by new carbon ceramic brakes.
A new Integrated Brake Control System is also on deck, and the Lamborghini Revuelto SV features a unique front fascia with a more pronounced apron, as well as black accents, dry carbon fiber, and the dedicated SV livery. A rear gurney flap, a fixed rear wing, a sports exhaust system with matte gray tips, and others are also on deck. The model is said to generate 80 percent more downforce compared to the standard Revuelto, and 10 percent more than the old Aventador SVJ (not the SV).
Photo: Instagram | lamborghinimiami And if these aren’t enough to convince you that you are looking at a serious supercar, then you should know that there are also modifications on the inside. Here, the steering wheel has been revised, and the vehicle has been equipped with carbon fiber door panels. The carbon fiber shelled seats are standard, and full-on carbon fiber racing seats are available as an option.
Production of the Lamborghini Revuelto SV is limited to 1,963 units, and this is a highly-customizable model straight from the factory. Take the pictured example, for instance, which benefits from multiple goodies signed by Ad Personam. The Raging Bull’s personalization division says that more than 400 color shades are available, joined by “an extensive range of customization options” that “allow owners to create a Lamborghini that reflects their vision.”
This particular ride is presented in Arancio Egon Matt, which is complemented by the Bronzo Serse accents on the SV logo, rear diffuser, Lamborghini lettering, and others, and the Nero Noctis livery. The wheels sport a Bronze Diamond Cut look, and the brake calipers visible from behind them have the same look.
Opening the door will reveal the Nero Cosmus Corsa-Tex and Arancio Dryope leather upholstery, as well as the Bronzo Oreadi embroidery that also includes the SV logo. Bronzo contrast stitching is part of the special optional makeover , alongside the Bronzo Serse painted accents, and the matte carbon fiber trim on the center console.
Photo: Instagram | lamborghinimiami This bright orange Lamborghini Revuelto SV, with its black details, bronze accents, dry carbon trim, and other goodies is definitely something to write home about, especially if you are into modern-day supercars. The Benjamins haven’t been mentioned in the social media post from Lamborghini Miami, but then again, you didn’t think that the sum would be discussed, did you?
Nevertheless, this is one pricey cookie , as it is estimated to start at almost $750,000, and that’s before factoring in any options, let alone the Ad Personam goodies available for it. A fully-specced example can end up costing close to the six-digit territory. As for the regular Revuelto, it kicks off at over $600,000.
Lamborghini’s Revuelto SV is not only a lot more advanced than the standard Revuelto, but also boasts more oomph. The naturally aspirated 6.5-liter V12 engine and the three axial flux electric motors, two at the front and one above the 8-speed DCT, work in concert to deliver a total of 1,050 hp (1,065 ps/783 kW). There is also a new 7.3 kWh battery pack on deck.
The Revuelto SV hits 62 mph (100 kph) in 2.4 seconds, and it is 0.1 seconds faster than the standard model. It also has 49 hp (50 ps/37 kW) more, though flat-out, it is a bit slower, as the top speed is 216 mph (348 kph) as opposed to 217 mph (350 kph) in the regular version of the brand’s new-gen flagship supercar.
It looks like Lamborghini is cooking up something more special for the Revuelto, because a mysterious tester was recently scooped in the open, and some believe that it could be the even more extreme SVJ. Guess we’ll have to wait and see if that is indeed the case or not. Meanwhile, what’s your take on this Ad Personam SV? Is it a yay o a yay? 2026 SEMA Show • 2027 Toyota Crown Signia Gets GT-S Concept Treatment for SEMA, Becomes a Sleek Wagon
With the Model S/X and Cybertruck Gone and No New Models, Tesla Is Disappearing Before Our Very Eyes
25 photos
Photo: Tesla, edited
We've already known that Tesla is no longer interested in car manufacturing, even before the Model S and Model X were pronounced dead in January. The demise of the Cybertruck only confirms this strategy shift. However, the fact that Tesla has no new car model in the pipeline shows that we're looking at what airplane pilots call "controlled flight into terrain."
When Musk announced in January during the Q4 2025 earnings call that the Model S and Model X would be retired, I knew that was only the beginning. At the time, Musk's plan to merge his companies into one giant corporation under his control was already well known. The first step of this plan was completed in February, when SpaceX bailed money-losing xAI . However, Tesla was a different beast.
The company had a solid market position, with a sane business, which Musk no longer controlled after selling shares to buy Twitter. Tesla was too big a fish to swallow even for SpaceX, which only recently posted its first profitable quarter. At the time, I argued that Musk doesn't want a strong Tesla; he'd be better served if it went into the ground. That's how I look at all the steps Musk and Tesla have been taking in 2026. And sure enough, he seems to be doing a remarkable job at making Tesla worthless.
From sustainable mobility to amazing abundance In 2022, Tesla appeared to be on top of the world, with demand through the roof and prices that defied gravity. Sales were booming, and Musk thought selling 20 million cars per year by 2030 was a no-brainer. A year later, market conditions changed, and sales dropped. This apparently caused great distress, because Musk made some erratic business decisions.
First, he decided that the economy was crashing and started preparing Tesla for the impact. Budgets were cut, and employees were fired, sometimes indiscriminately. Those who refused to let enough people go, such as Supercharger chief Rebecca Tinucci, were fired themselves . Others, including Drew Baglino, Tesla's Senior VP of Powertrain and Energy, and Martin Viecha, VP of Investor Relations, left voluntarily.
Second, Musk decided that EVs were no longer cool enough, and doubled down on autonomous driving efforts. Tesla had already announced plans to develop a humanoid robot in 2022. By the time cars became uncool, the Tesla Optimus program showed some progress, and Musk thought that driverless cars and robots, or robots on wheels and robots on legs, were the new future.
Photo: Tesla The "not a carmaker" mantra originated in this bizarre strategic pivot. As vehicle sales started to disappoint, Musk and his minions declared that deliveries were irrelevant, because Tesla is now an artificial intelligence and robotics company, not a carmaker. The bad thing is that Musk started believing this himself, and the company started moving away from vehicle manufacturing. Even worse was that Tesla sucked at both robots and autonomous driving.
First, they came for the Model S and X; then, they came for the Cybertruck The Gen-3 compact EV was the first victim of this change. Despite Musk's denial, the affordable EV, known as Project Redwood, was scrapped the moment Musk announced that Tesla moved its production from Mexico to Texas , in December 2023. When media outlets reported that the compact EV was no more, Musk called them liars and announced the Cybercab demo event.
Musk knew very well that Tesla had abandoned work on the Gen 3 platform. However, he pretended that affordable models were still on the menu. And they were, but not as new cars based on the revolutionary Gen-3 platform, but as stripped-down variants of the existing Model 3 and Model Y. Sold at lower prices, these energized Tesla vehicle sales in 2026, especially as the world faced an oil crisis that sent fuel prices into the stratosphere.
However, as car buyers started prioritizing their budgets, the market for $80k vehicles crashed, affecting sales of all other Tesla models. The Model S, Model X, and the Cybertruck were already counted in the "Other Vehicles" category. Now, this category started shrinking by the quarter. Unsurprisingly, Tesla announced in January that the Model S and Model X would stop production in the second quarter of 2026.
Photo: Tesla At the time, I wondered how long it would take before the Cybertruck shared their fate. The Model S and Model X were developed a long time ago, and development costs were already covered, probably many times over. However, the Cybertruck was a technological showcase, which was very expensive to develop. Selling it in low numbers must've cost Tesla a lot of money.
Now, Elon Musk confirmed that the Cybertruck will go to play with the Model S and Model X on the playground of automotive history. The move was hardly unexpected after Tesla announced to reservation holders in Australia and New Zealand in October that the right-hand variant has been canceled.
What's coming up next? The Model S, Model X, and even the Cybertruck were prime candidates for removal, considering their lackluster sales. Nobody expected them to last very long, even though some hoped that Tesla would remake the Cybertruck into a full-size SUV, or at least a traditionally-looking pickup truck. Despite these expectations, killing the Cybertruck caused quite a stir in the Tesla community.
Not because the carmaker decided to cut its losses and canceled the money-losing models. Every company makes such decisions, however painful they might be. Still, the Cybertruck, despite its many failures, was considered a symbol of Tesla engineering prowess. Killing it means that Tesla also kills its most promising technologies, including its first 800-volt platform, the 48-volt low-voltage system, steer-by-wire, and more.
Photo: Tesla There's another reason to mourn, though. Killing a vehicle model is not tragic. Not having anything to replace it or to add to the lineup is actually worse. No new vehicle model is in Tesla's pipeline, if we don't count the Roadster. However, the flying car is not a new vehicle; it's a PR stunt. Even if it were produced, it would not change anything for Tesla.
The Cybertruck's demise, especially after the Model S and Model X were scrapped, confirms that Tesla doesn't want to make cars anymore. It might not want to sell products to consumers at all, not just vehicles. And that makes a lot of people uncomfortable. What would they upgrade their Tesla to? A Cybercab? That's a hard pass for anyone who is not blinded by Musk's nonsense.
Model 3, which sells slightly worse than the Model Y, will absolutely be next on the chopping block. And how long will the Model Y survive? It's still a very popular EV today, but, like the Model 3, is underpinned by a ten-year-old vehicle platform. It will soon start failing new crash safety standards, and Tesla might decide that developing a successor is not worth investing in.
Is Tesla still alive? And why should it? It's already clear that Tesla will be folded into SpaceX and disappear as an entity altogether. SpaceX is not interested in its car manufacturing business, or insurance, or charging. "Where we're going, we don't need roads." It might find value in driverless cars like the Cybercab and robots and the software that powers them, but the rest? The best we can hope is a spin-off so that somebody else continues Tesla legacy.
Photo: Alcides Antunes/Instagram Even though Musk and his fans argue that the Cybercab is the future , this will not be the car people expect, and will likely sell in far smaller numbers than Musk wants us to believe. He already announced that Tesla would not sell the Cybercab to consumers, but to businesses. Outside big cities, nobody would want to hail a cab for their day-to-day errands. People very much want to own their cars, and most of them, even to drive them.
I am certain that the Cybercab, robots, and autonomous driving are just a fad and will be replaced with other moonshot projects. Musk is very good at selling new dreams when the old ones lose their appeal. We already see this with the Terafab chip-making project. In five years, there will be something else.
One thing is almost certain, though: Musk doesn't want Tesla to be very valuable. He wants SpaceX to buy it at the lowest possible price, strip it of its most valuable assets, and eventually sell the rest piece by piece. Tesla has already started outsourcing Supercharger buildout, so the process has started. The time is of the essence, so a move is expected to be announced next month during the annual shareholder meeting .

2024 Chevrolet Camaro SS Convertible Comes Up for Sale With 4k Miles and a Single Owner From New
76 photos
Photo: Motorcar Classics
New York-based Motorcar Classics probably thinks it has you covered if you're willing to write a rather small check for this 2024 Chevrolet Camaro SS that also has sensible looks, few miles on the odometer, and just one owner since new.
The mid-size General Motors sports car was born for the 1967 model year to compete in the newly established pony car subsegment alongside its platform sibling, the Pontiac Firebird, in a bid to steal the spotlight from the ultra-popular Ford Mustang. Initially, four generations were created, all with their own life stories, before production originally ended in 2002.
However, the fever of retro-modern American sports cars was just hitting with the S197 fifth-generation Ford Mustang launched for the 2005 model year, and General Motors had no choice but to follow in the footsteps of the third-generation 2008 Dodge Challenger, reintroducing the Camaro as a complete redesign on a brand-new platform for the 2010 model year.
The fifth and sixth generations were akin to the newer Ford Mustang, as they slowly transitioned to a more traditional sports car allure, while the Dodge Challenger remained steadfast in its retro looks, which came with mixed results – the Blue Oval managed to retain (slowly dwindling) interest for the Ford Mustang, which shows a tendency to regain its popularity over the past year, while GM had to pull the plug on the Camaro in December 2023, making the 2024 model year the final one so far for the iconic pony and muscle car.
Photo: Motorcar Classics While it may have lost some of its appeal among American muscle car fans, the Chevrolet Camaro remains a great option when it comes to playing with GM’s cool sports cars for anyone who thinks the C8 Chevrolet Corvette is too European after the switch to a mid-engine setup and too fixated on extreme performance with the latest ZR1 and ZR1X supercars.
So, if you want a nice-looking final model-year Chevrolet Camaro that also won’t break the bank, here’s a proposition from New York-based Motorcar Classics – a 2024 Chevrolet Camaro SS that can take its top off at a moment’s notice. The Convertible has just 4,176 original miles on the odometer, and it’s a single-owner car dressed in silver with a Jet Black leather interior.
It’s also the final model year of the iconic Camaro, and under the hood, this sixth-generation example has the classic 6.2-liter LT1 V8 engine producing an impressive 455 hp and 455 lb-ft of torque. The former owner wanted an engaging drive, and it’s fitted with the six-speed manual transmission, so you’ll have to row your own cogs – which is going to put a smile on your face if you know how to. If you don’t, get learning because it’s cool when such great cars are involved in the process.
Photo: Motorcar Classics “The interior is loaded with modern features and driver-focused amenities, while the power convertible top lets you enjoy open-air V8 performance at a moment's notice,” says the description, and it also has a spotless one-owner Carfax “report showing no accidents or damage and a documented history of regular dealership service.” As such, the car also has remaining factory warranty coverage, and it was also “superbly maintained and mechanically turnkey,” so it’s ready to make new memories on the spot.
Naturally, the dealership won’t give it away for free and instead asks for $52,500, or you can negotiate via the ‘make an offer’ tab in the online listing. So, what do you think? Yay or nay?
By the way, if you want some alternatives for around $50k, you clearly can’t have a C8 Chevy Corvette from new since the 2027 Stingray coupe retails from $71,300 with the new 6.7-liter V8 packing 535 hp and 520 lb-ft of torque. You would lose the opening top or pay more for the convertible, as well as the rear seats. Alternatively, you could break your vows and switch sides to the Blue Oval team and buy a brand-new S650 Ford Mustang .
Photo: Motorcar Classics The latter starts from around $33k for the EcoBoost Fastback, and if you want a matching Convertible, it’s going to be at least $41k – going out with the wind in your hair and no roof is pretty darn expensive these days, as it turns out. But you’re abandoning the massive 6.2-liter V8 for a smaller and turbocharged 2.3-liter EcoBoost inline-four packing 315 hp, a lot less than this Camaro SS. So, the best bet would be to switch to the GT version, which has the 5.0-liter Coyote V8.
Alas, while the GT Fastback starts at $49k, the Ford Mustang GT Convertible is only offered with the Premium trim level starting at over $58k – meaning that it’s more expensive than this Camaro SS. You do get at least 480 hp or 486 hp when equipped with the Active valve performance exhaust, so you have to see if the higher pony count is worth the additional cash. So, what do you think – yay or nay?

2026 SEMA Show • Hybrid Honda Passport Throws More HP in Baja Racing Than Any Other 9.0-Liter V8-Powered Trophy Truck
Here’s How Much a 2024 Lamborghini Urus Performante Costs After 9,000 Miles
14 photos
Photo: Instagram | motorcarsofchicago
Does the Lamborghini Urus still keep you up at night for whatever reason? Well, we won’t judge you if it does, because it is the Raging Bull’s most popular model ever. On top of that, it’s a family-friendly machine aimed at daily drives, which definitely goes like stink.
The family comprises a single member at the moment. It is the Urus SE Performante unveiled earlier this year, and while it may be an extremely important model for the brand, it does not get that much attention. It has 801 hp (812 ps/597 kW) and 738 lb-ft (1,000 Nm) of torque in total from its 4-liter twin-turbo plug-in hybrid V8, and this makes it 12 hp (12 ps/9 kW) more powerful than the Urus SE. It is also 144 hp (146 ps/107 kW) punchier than the S and Performante versions of the exotic crossover.
Lamborghini’s new Urus SE Performante , which will keep the Urus on the appealing side of the segment for as long as possible, as a successor is nowhere in sight just yet, takes only 3.3 seconds to hit 62 mph (100 kph) from a standstill. And while that may be an 0.1-second improvement over the Urus SE, it cannot beat the Performante. But it does something the latter cannot do, as it does not benefit from an electrified powertrain, namely travel for 37 miles (60 km) or so on electric power alone.
Some say that the Lamborghini Urus Performante remains the sweet spot of the series, even if it is dead and buried, and if you believe the same, then you may want to keep reading, because the example pictured in the gallery above is searching for a new home in the United States of America as we speak. As mentioned in the title, it is a 2024 model year car, and has in the region of 9,000 miles (~14,500 km) on the clock. Therefore, it is a low-mileage example, and it definitely looks very good both inside and out.
Photo: Instagram | motorcarsofchicago This Lamborghini Urus Performante features a purple paint finish on the outside with a satin look, has plenty of black details for contrast, and rides on a set of bi-tone alloys that combine silver and copper. Shod in sticky tires from Pirelli and decorated with the Raging Bull’s emblem in the middle, the alloys spin around the black brake calipers, which feature Lamborghini branding on them in white. This machine also features tinted windows, though the interior has opened up to the camera.
Step inside and you will see plenty of Alcantara upholstery in black, joined by black leather and some white leather strips for a bit of contrast here and there. The vehicle also features white stitching for more contrast, has the Urus name embroidered into the seatbacks, the Raging Bull’s logo on the integrated headrests, and the Performante emblem on the outer bolsters. The dashboard panel was wrapped in Alcantara, and there is plenty of carbon fiber trim on deck, as well as a red 12 o’clock marker on the steering wheel.
For what it’s worth, it seems that there isn’t anything wrong with this particular Lamborghini Urus Performante , as it looks pretty much like it just left the showroom floor. The vendor hasn’t mentioned any known flaws, but then again, it did not have much to say about it, and it chose to keep the powertrain details away from the social media post embedded at the bottom of the page.
Photo: Instagram | motorcarsofchicago However, we will remind you that this model, as well as the Urus S, which is also dead and buried, have 657 horsepower (490 kW/666 ps) available via the right pedal, and 627 lb-ft (850 Nm) of torque. According to the spec sheet, the Urus Performante needs just 3.3 seconds to hit 62 mph (100 kph) from a standstill, and this makes it two-tenths of a second faster than the S, which uses the same 4.0-liter twin-turbo V8 engine in the same configuration. Flat-out, it will do 190 mph (306 kph), whereas the S will top out at 189 mph (305 kph).
In today’s used car market, the Lamborghini Urus Performante usually costs from $250,000 to over $320,000 in the United States of America, though a later model year with only a few miles under its belt in pristine condition can change hands for almost $400,000. So, how much do you think the pictured 2024 model year crossover with its 9,000 miles or so is worth? Unless you said $329,995, then you are wrong, because this was the asking price at the time of writing.
The vehicle is advertised by @motorcarsofchicago on social media. The vendor accepts trade-ins, offers financing, and you know what to do if you want this machine, don’t you? But realistically speaking, is this Lamborghini Urus Performante worth $330K in your opinion? View this post on Instagram A post shared by Motor Cars of Chicago (@motorcarsofchicago)
